strengths: Addresses an interesting and timely problem: training-free video reasoning segmentation using the latent localization behavior of MLLMs, avoiding task-specific finetuning.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually simple and practically appealing: attention rollout, object-background contrastive fusion, video-frame complementary fusion, and SAM2 prompting form a coherent end-to-end method.
Empirical coverage is relatively broad, with results across multiple MLLM families and five VOS/reasoning VOS datasets, including both attention-only masks and SAM-refined masks.

Ablations are useful and mostly support the main components: contrastive fusion, video-frame fusion, multi-scale processing, vision-aware rollout normalization, threshold choices, and attention consistency scoring all receive quantitative analysis.
The paper is clear about some limitations, including failure cases involving large objects, very small/briefly appearing objects, and thin structures.
Results with Qwen2.5-VL-7B are strong for a training-free method, especially on Ref-DAVIS and ReasonVOS, and in some settings are competitive with trained MLLM-SAM systems.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: the core operations are prompt-based attention differencing, attention rollout variants, averaging video/frame maps, and SAM2 prompt filtering. These are sensible but not deeply new algorithmically.

The comparison to baselines is not fully clean. The Loc-Head comparison appears to use the authors' SAM prompting pipeline for subsequent comparisons, which makes it difficult to separate gains from DecAF itself versus gains from the new SAM2 prompting/filtering procedure.

The TAM and Loc-Head adaptations are described as fragile and substantially modified, but the paper provides limited evidence that these reproductions are fair or optimally tuned. Some reported TAM numbers are extremely low, raising concern that the baseline setup may disadvantage prior methods.

The claim of being comparable to training-based methods is only partially supported: the best results are competitive on some datasets, but still lag recent trained methods on ReVOS, MeViS, and Ref-YTVOS, sometimes by substantial margins.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code will be available but gives no actual repository, and important implementation details such as exact preprocessing, prompts for all models, SAM2 propagation settings, computational cost, and model-specific handling are not fully specified.

The method depends on correct object-category extraction by the MLLM, but the paper does not quantify category prediction accuracy or analyze how category errors propagate into background subtraction and SAM prompting.

Several hyperparameters and design choices, including rollout start layer and SAM thresholds, appear selected empirically; although some robustness is shown, there is limited discussion of validation protocol or whether settings were tuned on test sets.

The attention consistency score can penalize correct large-object masks and briefly visible small objects, which are important cases in video segmentation; this limitation may affect practical reliability.

The paper would benefit from stronger positioning against broader training-free/open-vocabulary segmentation alternatives beyond MLLM-attention methods, such as grounding-plus-SAM pipelines or zero-shot video segmentation systems.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: training-free video reasoning/referring segmentation using existing MLLMs and SAM2, which is practically attractive if reliable.

The proposed decomposition into object/background contrastive attention and video/frame complementary attention is simple and intuitive, and the ablations generally show that each component improves the reported metrics.
The evaluation covers several datasets and multiple MLLM backbones, which is broader than many training-free grounding papers.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. Most of the method is a heuristic combination of known attention rollout, prompt contrast, thresholding, and SAM/SAM2 prompting; the paper does not provide a strong conceptual or theoretical contribution beyond engineering these pieces together.

The empirical claims are overstated. The method is described as comparable to training-based approaches, but it is clearly behind recent strong supervised methods on several datasets, especially ReVOS, MeViS, and Ref-YTVOS. The comparisons also mix different MLLMs and segmentation backbones, making attribution difficult.

Baseline fairness is a major concern. Loc-Head and TAM are adapted/reproduced under the authors' protocol, and the appendix explicitly describes changing baseline prompting/evaluation details. It is unclear whether the baselines are implemented in their strongest or intended form, and the very poor TAM numbers raise questions about whether the comparison is meaningful.

The method depends heavily on prompt templates, object-category extraction, thresholds, attention normalization choices, sampled frames, and SAM2 post-processing. These are all potential hidden hyperparameters, yet the paper gives limited evidence of robustness beyond a few threshold sweeps.

The training-free framing is somewhat misleading in terms of practical cost and dependence on pretrained systems: performance relies on large MLLMs plus SAM2, but runtime, memory, number of model calls per video/frame, and failure modes under long videos are not adequately analyzed.

The evaluation lacks deeper diagnostic evidence. There is no statistical significance, limited analysis by object size/absence/multi-object cases beyond qualitative examples, and no convincing study separating language reasoning ability from segmentation/post-processing quality.

The paper's central mechanism assumes attention maps are reliable explanations for localization, but this assumption is not sufficiently justified. Attention rollout is known to be noisy, and the proposed fixes remain heuristic.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code will be available, but the submission does not appear to provide enough implementation detail to reproduce all preprocessing, model-specific resolution handling, frame sampling, SAM2 propagation, and baseline adaptations reliably.

Writing and presentation have notable issues: inconsistent naming between Decoupled and Decomposed Attention Fusion, grammar/formatting problems, crowded tables, and some unsupported phrasing such as claims that the method 'clearly manifests' effectiveness.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: training-free video reasoning segmentation with MLLMs, avoiding costly model-specific fine-tuning while still targeting referring and reasoning VOS settings.

The core method is simple, well-motivated, and practically appealing: attention rollout is strengthened with vision-aware normalization, contrastive object-background fusion, video-frame complementary fusion, and attention-guided SAM2 prompting.
The empirical evaluation is fairly broad, covering multiple datasets, MLLM families, model sizes, and both attention-only masks and SAM-refined dense masks.

Results are strong for a training-free approach. In particular, DecAF substantially improves over training-free baselines such as TAM and Loc-Head, and in some cases approaches or exceeds training-based methods on Ref-DAVIS and ReasonVOS.

The ablations are useful and support the main design choices, including object-background contrast, video-frame fusion, rollout normalization, SAM prompting thresholds, and attention consistency scoring.
The appendix includes qualitative examples and failure cases, which helps make the behavior of the method more interpretable.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The method is a thoughtful composition of attention rollout, contrastive prompting, multi-scale/frame-video fusion, and SAM prompting, but most ingredients are conceptually familiar. The paper could better distinguish the genuinely new technical contribution from engineering integration.

The comparison to prior training-free methods is somewhat delicate. Loc-Head and TAM are image-oriented or token-sensitive methods adapted to this setting, and the paper reports several modifications or reproduction choices. This raises questions about whether the baselines are fully optimized and fairly matched.

Some experimental reporting has inconsistencies or unclear details. For example, at least one table entry appears numerically inconsistent with the reported mean metric, and implementation details such as sampling, thresholds, rollout layer choices, and prompt/model variance could be specified more rigorously.

The method depends on several heuristic thresholds and prompt templates. Although some robustness analysis is provided, the approach may still be sensitive to object category prediction, prompt wording, frame sampling, and the particular attention behavior of each MLLM.

The claim of being comparable to training-based methods is only partially supported. DecAF is very competitive on some datasets, but remains clearly below recent trained methods on others such as ReVOS, MeViS, and Ref-YTVOS.

The evaluation would be stronger with more analysis of computational cost. The method invokes MLLMs multiple times for object/background and video/frame attention and then runs SAM2 tracklet propagation, which may be expensive relative to trained segmentation models.

Failure-mode analysis is present but limited. The paper would benefit from a more systematic breakdown by object size, temporal absence, multi-object cases, long videos, thin structures, and category prediction errors.

Reproducibility is not fully established in the manuscript. The abstract says code will be available but the shown manuscript does not provide an actual link, and exact prompts, preprocessing, model versions, and evaluation scripts are important for this kind of training-free method.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: training-free video reasoning/referring object segmentation using existing MLLMs and SAM2, avoiding task-specific fine-tuning.

The proposed DecAF pipeline is simple, modular, and intuitive: contrastive object/background attention fusion, video/frame complementary fusion, vision-aware rollout normalization, and attention-guided SAM2 prompting.
Empirical evaluation is fairly broad, covering multiple MLLM families and sizes and five datasets, including both referring VOS and reasoning VOS benchmarks.

Results are consistently stronger than prior training-free attention-based baselines, with especially large gains on reasoning-heavy datasets; the paper also includes useful ablations for fusion components, rollout variants, thresholds, prompt variants, and model scale.

The appendix is comparatively rich, with prompt templates, qualitative successes/failures, robustness checks, native grounding comparisons, and analysis of multiple-object and non-explicit expression cases.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is moderate: the main mechanisms are prompt-based attention subtraction, averaging video/frame attention, thresholding, and SAM2 filtering. These are effective but conceptually incremental over attention rollout and attention-as-prompt work.

Comparisons to training-based methods are somewhat hard to interpret because models differ substantially in backbone MLLM, SAM/SAM2 use, sampling strategy, and temporal modules. The claim of being comparable or superior to training-based methods may be stronger than the evidence supports.

The handling of baselines raises concerns: Loc-Head is adapted and in some cases evaluated with the authors' SAM prompting pipeline, while TAM is reported as extremely weak under this protocol. More direct reproduction details, official-code parity, and baseline sensitivity analysis would strengthen confidence.

The method requires many MLLM forward passes for object/background, video/frame, and sampled frames plus SAM2 propagation, but runtime, memory, and cost are not reported. This is important for a training-free method whose practical appeal depends on inference efficiency.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: implementation details are scattered, the apparent code link is missing/blank, and several choices such as exact sampling, prompt execution, NMS details, resolution settings, and threshold selection would need clearer specification.

The method remains heuristic-heavy, with fixed thresholds, prompt-dependent category extraction, mean/Otsu masking, and attention consistency scoring. Although ablations show robustness in some settings, there is limited analysis of when these heuristics fail systematically.

Failure cases reveal limitations for large objects with sparse attention, tiny/brief objects, thin structures, and part-level segmentation where SAM2 may segment the whole object rather than the intended part. These limitations are not fully addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: training-free video reasoning segmentation using existing MLLMs and SAM2, which is practically appealing if reliable.
The method is simple and modular, combining attention rollout, object-background contrast, video-frame fusion, and attention-guided SAM2 prompting in an understandable pipeline.
The empirical section covers multiple datasets and several MLLM backbones, and includes useful ablations for the fusion components, rollout variant, SAM thresholds, and tracklet scoring.
The appendix includes additional analyses on prompt robustness, native Qwen2.5-VL grounding baselines, multiple similar objects, part-level cases, and failure examples.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Most ingredients are straightforward combinations of attention rollout, contrastive prompting/subtraction, multi-scale frame/video fusion, thresholding, and SAM2 prompting. The paper does not provide a particularly deep technical insight beyond a set of heuristics that work reasonably well.

The main claims are overstated. The method is described as comparable to or better than training-based methods, but the results are mixed: it underperforms strong training-based methods on MeViS, Ref-YTVOS, and much of ReVOS, while the strongest claims rely heavily on ReasonVOS and selected comparisons.

The evaluation is not fully convincing. The performance of direct attention masks is very low, and much of the final gain appears to come from SAM2 plus the proposed candidate filtering/prompting pipeline. This makes it hard to isolate whether the paper demonstrates meaningful MLLM localization or mostly a good SAM2 prompting heuristic.

The comparison to prior training-free methods raises fairness concerns. Loc-Head is extensively modified or reprocessed with the authors' own prompting pipeline, while TAM is argued to fail under a particular adaptation. These baselines may be reasonable attempts, but the paper needs a cleaner and more neutral protocol.

The method contains many heuristic choices: prompt templates, object-category extraction, Gaussian smoothing, min-max normalization choices, layer selection, threshold values, attention consistency scoring, and NMS rules. The ablations help, but the design still feels brittle and insufficiently principled.

Reproducibility is weak in the manuscript as given: the code link is blank, compute/runtime costs are not reported, implementation details are incomplete for several steps, and there is no clear discussion of how hyperparameters were selected without test-set tuning.

The paper relies on attention maps as localization evidence without adequately engaging with known limitations of attention as explanation or testing whether the attention truly reflects causal visual evidence rather than post-hoc correlation.

The writing and presentation have several issues, including inconsistent naming between Decoupled/Decomposed Attention Fusion, typos, unclear formulas, and occasional unsupported assertions. These do not make the paper unreadable, but they reduce confidence in a top-tier submission.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and relevant problem: training-free video reasoning segmentation using existing MLLMs and SAM2, avoiding costly joint fine-tuning.

The core method is simple and well motivated: contrastive object-background attention fusion addresses attention sinks, video-frame fusion combines temporal context with spatial detail, and attention-guided SAM2 prompting converts coarse maps into dense masks.

The empirical results are strong for a training-free method. DecAF consistently improves over Loc-Head and TAM across multiple MLLM families, and the gains on reasoning-heavy datasets such as ReasonVOS are especially compelling.

The paper includes useful ablations for object-background fusion, video-frame fusion, multi-scale processing, rollout variants, SAM prompting thresholds, attention consistency scoring, model scaling, and prompt robustness.

The qualitative analysis and failure cases are helpful, showing where the method succeeds on temporal/world-knowledge queries and where it struggles with small, large, thin, or briefly appearing objects.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. The method combines attention rollout, contrastive prompting/subtraction, multi-scale frame-video fusion, and SAM2 prompting; these are sensible engineering choices, but the conceptual advance over prior attention-as-localization work is incremental.

Some comparisons are not fully clean. The paper modifies or replaces parts of Loc-Head with the proposed SAM prompting pipeline for fairness, but this also makes it harder to separate gains from better attention maps versus gains from the new SAM2 prompting and filtering procedure.

Claims of being comparable or superior to training-based methods should be tempered. Performance is excellent on ReasonVOS and Ref-DAVIS, but DecAF remains below stronger trained methods on MeViS and Ref-YTVOS, and comparisons involve different base MLLMs, sampling strategies, and segmentation backbones.

The method relies on access to internal attention tensors and on model-specific visual token layouts/resolutions, which may limit applicability to closed MLLMs or architectures with different attention implementations.

Computational cost is insufficiently analyzed. The pipeline requires multiple MLLM forward passes for object/background prompts at video and frame levels, plus SAM2 propagation; a runtime and memory comparison to training-free and trained baselines is needed.

Several hyperparameters and design choices, such as rollout starting layer, Gaussian smoothing, point-query threshold, tracklet threshold, and attention consistency formulation, appear selected empirically. Robustness is studied, but the method still has several coupled heuristics.

The attention consistency score can incorrectly reject valid masks when attention covers only part of a large object or when targets are small/brief, which is acknowledged but remains a meaningful limitation for real video segmentation use cases.

Reproducibility would benefit from more explicit implementation details, including exact frame sampling, resolutions per model, Gaussian kernel settings, SAM2 propagation settings, and whether any validation data influenced hyperparameter choices.
